newsitem.title: CHINA: Monetary boss vows to hit speculators against HK$.
newsitem.headline: Monetary boss vows to hit speculators against HK$.

text.p: Monetary boss Joseph Yam said on Monday there had been a lot of "hot air" about speculation against the Hong Kong dollar and vowed to punish anyone betting against the currency.
"This situation is actually very stable and I feel very comfortable about it," he told a news briefing.
"These sort of activities are caused by people who are playing around with the market and shorting the currency. They have to borrow the currency eventually and that's where we catch them," he said.
Yam, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive, said there had been speculation against the local dollar on Thursday and Friday but that it had not been very intense.
"A lot of activity, all small deals. I would say US$20 to US$30 million but if you had big speculators you'd be talking about US$200 million actually. Those are big deals," he said.
Some money dealers have suggested that the Hong Kong dollar could be the next Asian currency to face a sustained speculative attack.
It is the last major currency in Asia which is still pegged to the U.S. dollar. Other currencies around the region have been forced from their pegs, effectively devalued, since early July.

The Thai baht has depreciated by more than 30 percent, the Indonesian rupiah more than 20 percent, the Malaysian ringgit more than 10 percent, the Philippine Peso about 14 percent and the Singapore dollar by six percent since July 1.
Yam compared the scale of events last week to a speculative swoop in July when Hong Kong spent US$1 billion in a single day to defend its currency.
Hong Kong officials boosted later that they had roasted the July speculators. Of events last week, Yam said: "In so far as Friday is concerned, we won the game."
Yam said local banks helped by pushing up interbank rates to 8-1/2 to nine percent, which he described as a risk premium for lending ahead of a long three-day weekend.
Banks had been warned not to call on the Monetary Authority too frequently as lendor of last resort or this could indicate they were involved in speculation against the Hong Kong dollar, he said.
"I reserve our right ... not to apply the standard liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), at this point 6.5 percent, to those people that have been frequently using the LAF," he said.
"We have the discretion to charge a higher rate or lower rate or much higher rate. That's why I refer to possibly 12 percent or even 60 percent if there were a need," he added.

His message to banks coming too frequently to the Monetary Authority for funds was "beware ... we may actually selectively charge higher rates for those banks that have been using that facility in a big way."
Yam said that so far the Monetary Authority had applied only the 6.5 percent rate.
The move against the Hong Kong dollar on Friday was cited as one factor behind a sharp slide in the Hang Seng share index, which closed 2.43 percent or 400.83 points down at 16,096.88.
Yam was concerned persistent "hot air" about speculation against the Hong Kong dollar could prompt Hong Kong people to shift their assets elsewhere.

"If alternatively it's those people who have Hong Kong dollar assets ... losing confidence in the Hong Kong dollar, selling the Hong Kong dollar ... the situation may be a little more difficult but we are not seeing that," he said.

Hong Kong's foreign currency reserves at June 30 stood at US$82 billion and a local newspaper said on Saturday that China was prepared to use $50 billion of its foreign reserves to defend the Hong Kong currency.
China reassumed control of the territory on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule. -- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6441
